questions.q: A file called notice.txt is already there. Read the whole of it in one go, close it, and display exactly what was in it and nothing of your own.

teach.say: open() takes a file name and a mode, and 'r' means read. .read() brings the whole file back as one string, and .close() lets go of it.

brief: Nothing is typed in, and the program only reads the file.
questions.starter: # read it all, close it, print it

files.notice.txt:
Fire drill Friday
Meet on the field

tests.why: Both lines come out of one .read(). If you only got the first line you used .readline(), which stops after one.
A one-line file reads just as easily. If nothing printed, you read the file into a variable but never printed it.

files.notice.txt:
Bus bay 4
Leaves at 2 15
Bring your pass

tests.why: Three lines, one .read(). If you printed a heading of your own as well, the output will not match - print only the file.

questions.fb: open() needs the file name and the mode. 'r' means read. .read() brings back the whole file as one string, newlines and all, and .close() lets go of it.

questions.q: A file called log.txt is already there and may be empty. Read it and count every character, newlines included, then display characters [the count].
brief: Nothing is typed in, the program only reads the file, and an empty file holds 0 characters.

tests.why: Three letters and the newline on the end make 4. If you got 3 you stripped the newline off, and the brief says to count it.
An empty file is still a file. .read() gives back an empty string, so the length is 0 - a program that crashes or prints nothing here assumed there would always be something to read.
Nine characters, a newline, nine characters, a newline is 20. If you got 18 you counted the lines separately and lost the newlines.
The last line of a file does not have to end with a newline. If this gave 2 you are adding one on yourself.

questions.fb: len() on what .read() gave back counts the characters in the whole file. Newlines are real characters, which is why a file usually looks longer than you expect.

questions.q: A file called rota.txt is already there and may be empty. Read its first line only, close the file and strip the newline off, then display first [that line], then length [how many characters] on the next line.

teach.say: .readline() reads up to the next newline only, so what comes back still has \n on the end. .strip() takes it off.

brief: Nothing is typed in, and the program only reads the file.
questions.starter: # one line only, then strip it

tests.why: Only the first line is wanted, and Monday Ava is 10 characters. If Tuesday Ben appeared too you used .read() or .readlines() instead of .readline().
A file with one line in it. A length of 8 means the newline is still counted, so the line was never stripped.
An empty file gives .readline() an empty string back, not an error. A program that crashes here assumed there is always a first line to read.

files.rota.txt:
Wednesday Dev
Thursday Eve
Friday Fay

tests.why: The first line of a long file is still just the first line. If a blank line appeared between the two outputs, the newline is still stuck on the end of what you printed.

questions.fb: .readline() reads up to and including the next newline, so what comes back has \n on the end. .strip() takes that off, along with any stray spaces, and the length shows whether it really went.

questions.q: A file called names.txt is already there with one name per line, and may be empty. Read it and display lines [how many lines], then one line per name in the form [position] [name], counting from 1.
brief: Nothing is typed in, the program only reads the file, and each name's newline is stripped.
questions.starter: # how many, then each one numbered

tests.why: Three names, numbered from 1. If your numbers ran 0 1 2 you used the list position straight, and the brief asks you to start at 1.
One name is one line. If the count said 3 you may have counted characters rather than lines.
An empty file gives .readlines() an empty list, so the count is 0 and the loop simply does not run. A crash here means you went straight for lines[0] without checking.
If each name printed with a blank line after it, the newline from the file is still attached - strip it before printing.

questions.fb: .readlines() gives you a list with one string per line, so len() tells you how many lines there are. Each string still ends with \n until you strip it.

questions.q: Ask the user for a title. Make a file called report.txt, write the title on one line and ready on the next, and close it. Then read report.txt back in one go and display it.

teach.say: Mode 'w' opens a file for writing. .write() adds no newline of its own, so you put the \n in yourself.

brief: There is no file to start with, and .write() adds no newline of its own.
questions.starter: # write it, close it, read it back

tests.why: The file has to exist before you can read it back. A crash saying no such file means the write never happened, or you opened the wrong name.
The title comes from input, the word ready is fixed. If both ended up on one line you forgot the \n after the title - .write() adds nothing of its own.
If the output was empty, you read the file before closing it after writing - what you wrote may still be waiting to be saved.

questions.fb: print() puts a newline on the end for you. .write() does not, so you have to write \n yourself when you want a new line in the file.

questions.q: Ask the user for an entry. Open the file stock.txt in write mode, which empties whatever it held, write that entry on a line of its own and close it. Read it back and display [every line], then lines [how many].
brief: stock.txt is already there and may already hold lines.
Strip each line's newline before printing it.
questions.starter: # write mode, then count what survived

tests.why: The two old lines are gone, because write mode empties the file first. If you still see old bolts you opened it with 'a' instead of 'w'.
Writing to an empty file works the same way. If the count said 0 you read the file before closing it.
Three old lines, still only one left. A count of 4 means the new entry was added to the end rather than replacing the file.
Writing the same text that was already there still leaves one line, not two.

questions.fb: Opening a file with 'w' empties it the moment it opens, even if you then write nothing. That is the difference between 'w' and 'a', and it is easy to lose work to.

questions.q: Ask the user for a name and append it to the file visits.txt on a line of its own, without losing the names already there. Then read the whole file back and display latest [the last name], then total [how many lines].

teach.say: Mode 'a' appends: it opens the file with the writing point already at the end, so nothing already in there is thrown away.

brief: visits.txt is already there and may be empty.
Strip the newline off the last line before printing it.
questions.starter: # add to the end, then report on the whole log

tests.why: Two names were there, so adding one makes three. A total of 1 means you opened the file with 'w', which wiped Ava and Ben.
Append mode works on an empty file too, and the one name you added is also the last line. A crash here means you went for lines[1] rather than the end of the list.
The new name goes on the end, so the last line is the one just added, not Eve. Printing Eve means you took lines[0].
If a blank line appeared between the two lines of output, the newline is still on the end of the line you read - strip it before printing.

questions.fb: 'a' for append opens the file with the writing point already at the end, so what you write is added. 'w' would throw the whole log away first.

questions.q: Ask the user for a name to find in the file members.txt, which holds one name,age record per line. Look at every record and display [name] is [age], or not a member when none matches, then checked [how many you looked at].

teach.say: A record is one line made of fields. Strip the newline first, then .split(',') breaks the line into a list of those fields.

brief: members.txt is already there and may be empty, and the program only reads it.
Look at every record, even after one has matched.
questions.starter: # one record per line, one name to find

tests.why: Ben is the second record, and all three were looked at. If a blank line appeared before the checked line, you split the record before stripping it, so the newline is still part of the age field.
Nobody matches, so the message is printed once after the loop. Printing it three times means the message sits inside the loop instead of after it.
An empty file has no records, so nobody matches and nothing was checked. A crash here means you read a record before checking there was one.
A file with a single record still has to be searched. If nothing was found, the loop may be stopping before it looks at the only line.
The last record must be checked too. Printing not a member here means the loop gave up as soon as the first line failed to match.

questions.fb: A record is one line made of fields. .split(',') breaks the line into a list of those fields, so fields[0] is the name and fields[1] is the age.

questions.q: A file called scores.txt is already there, holding one name,score record per line, and may be empty. Read it and display no scores when it holds none, or total [every score added up], then best [the highest scorer's name].
brief: Nothing is typed in, and the program only reads the file.
The earlier record wins a tie for the highest score.
questions.starter: # the total and the best of one column

tests.why: 7 plus 9 plus 4 is 20, and Ben's 9 is the highest. A total of 794 means the score field was joined as text instead of turned into a number with int().
One record is its own total and its own best. If the best came out blank, the highest is only being updated when a later score beats a starting value you never set.
No records at all. A program that prints total 0 here, or crashes looking for the highest, assumed the file always has data in it.
A tie goes to the first one in the file, so the test for the highest has to be strictly greater than, not greater than or equal to.
Scores of zero are still records. If best came out blank, you started the highest at 0 and nothing ever beat it - start from the first record instead.

questions.fb: Totalling a column means reading each record, pulling out one field, turning it into a number and adding it on. The running total starts at 0 before the loop, never inside it.

questions.q: A file called sales.txt holds one item,quantity,price record per line. Make a file called report.txt holding a line of [item] [quantity times price] for each record, then total [all those values added up]. Close it, read it back and display the whole of it.

teach.say: One file can be open for reading while another is open for writing, which is how a report is built from data.

brief: sales.txt is already there and may be empty, and nothing is typed in.
questions.starter: # one file in, another out, then read it back

tests.why: 3 times 50 is 150, 2 times 120 is 240, and the two make 390. If the total line came first, it was written before the loop rather than after.
One record, so its value is also the total. Two identical lines is right here - do not skip the total line just because it matches.
No records, so nothing is written for them, but the total line still has to be written. A program that writes nothing and then reads an empty report prints nothing at all.
The records must come out in the order they were in the file. If the values were right but the total was 0, the running total is being reset inside the loop.
A quantity of zero is worth zero, and the record still gets a line of its own in the report.

questions.fb: Reading one file and writing another is the usual shape of a report. Only what you print is seen, so reading the report back is how you prove you really wrote it.

questions.q: Ask the user for a limit. The file readings.txt holds one sensor,reading record per line: make a file called alerts.txt holding a line of [sensor] [reading] for each reading above the limit. Then read alerts.txt back and display [every line], then alerts [how many].
brief: readings.txt is already there and may be empty, and the limit is a whole number.
Make alerts.txt even when nothing matches, and a reading equal to the limit does not count.
questions.starter: # filter out, then read the new file back

tests.why: 35 and 28 are both over 25, and t1 is not. If t1 appeared too, the readings are being compared as text - '20' is bigger than '2' as text, so int() is needed.
Nothing is over 50, so alerts.txt is written empty and the count is 0. A crash here means you tried to read a file you only opened when there was something to put in it - open it either way.
No readings at all, so no alerts. The count line still has to be printed.
41 is above 40 by one. If this was missed you used >= on the wrong side, or compared the limit to the sensor name instead of the reading.
Exactly the limit is not above the limit, so nothing is written. This is the boundary - >= instead of > fails only here.
Two separate records can hold the same reading and both count. If only one line printed, you stopped the loop at the first match.

questions.fb: This is the whole pattern in one program: read records in, decide about each one, write the chosen ones out, then read the new file back. Opening alerts.txt before the loop is what makes the empty case work.
